segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK, my name is Guy Soldier. I come from Jay to the north. You know where Jay is?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: We went there just yesterday.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, were y'all looking around?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I get a little time now that the kids have grown up, I am by myself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, you're by yourself?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I'm not married. I never have married, I just had kids. They came.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, really? So, you can just go when you want and come back when you want.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Where they call Tulsa, that is where two of them live, and another one in Arkansas. Evansville. They say another lives out towards their mom’s. There are four, three girls and one boy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your grandchildren, how many are there?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: You won’t believe it, but there are twenty.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Twenty.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Twenty? Oh, really.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Ain’t it? They were busy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gaw. It cost you at Christmas.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I hide when they say we are going to be there at this time. I say OK but I'm not home when they get there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is your name in Cherokee and in English?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: In English, Larry Don Ketcher is my name. My dad named me in Cherokee. It is Kvtli in Cherokee. They would call me Coon Ketcher.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Kvtli digvneyesgi, what were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: My dad’s name was Jimmy Ketcher, and in Cherokee his name was Uhvluga. My mother used to be an Adair, Sally Adair, and when she married my dad, she became Ketcher. And in Cherokee, they just called her Selu.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your grandmother and grandfather, what were their names?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: All of us children used to call our grandmother Mom. People were amused that we called her Mom.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: And our mom, we just called her by her name.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Your grandmother would always be involved in ball games. I remember her all the time. I don’t think she ever missed.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: She was good friends with Little Jack.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, really.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Little Jack would come to our house. My dad and mom had lots of chickens. He would come to get eggs. He would take a lot with him. “Boy, my family are always hungry for eggs,” he would say, Little Jack. Wale was my grandmother’s Cherokee name, and her husband I never saw, he was already passed, he was older than my grandmother. My grandmother was about fourteen, and he was already over forty. He had already been married first. His name was Thomas Adair. That’s all I know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Thomas Adair.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: My grandmother was from Bell. She was a Jones. When she got married, she became Mariyah Adair.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? When were you born and where was it that you were born? Here at the hospital?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Here in Tahlequah at the old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where they call Hastings?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah, it was little then. They would admit them. A long time ago, the youngest was born. Mom stayed in there for a week while they watched her.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: And now...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They let them go real quick. What year were you born?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Sixty one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sixty one, yeah you said a little bit ago. Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Rocky Mountain. Rocky Mountain, as far as I know. I was about five or six before I knew anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: It wasn’t like when they start at the age of three nowadays. It wasn’t like that then. I was six before I started school. It wasn’t until then that I heard them speak English. There was a Cherokee translator working there. The teacher was white. That Cherokee knew what that white was saying, so when the teacher said something, they would translate it and tell us what she was saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Who was it that translated?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: It was, ah, Foster, Sue Foster. She was Charles Foster’s mother.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, I remember her.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: And the teacher was from this way. She was teaching at Rocky Mountain. Gladyce Young was her name. She was already an old lady then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That Foster, you said Charles Foster? I knew him long ago.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He used to be a preacher.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah. What happened to him?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: He’s still alive.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s still alive, ain’t it? I see him sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I haven’t seen him in a long time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He looks like he is real sickly now, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: There is another. I think he is the oldest. Bill I think is his name, Bill Foster. And another is Kenneth, I think. Kenneth is the last born. Where the Cherokee do things, I think that’s where Kenneth works.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you learn English easy?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I haven’t learned it all yet.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You finished learning English?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: If I am talking to someone white, and I can’t understand, I start talking in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He will be sitting there and don’t understand.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I will run out of English, I tell them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s probably changed a lot where you lived and grew up.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: It has changed, I feel sorry for those that are growing up nowadays. They could not ever see what I have seen growing up. They have come through hard times. Grandmother, my dad and mom, I can still see the things that they did a long time ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They worked hard.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah, they got paid very little. They would hoe strawberries, and they would pick tomatoes where the whites were, where Bairds is. They worked there a lot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, they worked there.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Where Bairds is, they would work till noon and barely make four dollars. Back then, there were nine of us, and Mom and Dad had a hard life. Nowadays, I will get up early and sit outside sometimes, and think about it, just like it happened yesterday. I know things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, your mind still goes there, thinking about things?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How you came.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Nowadays, these kids that are growing up, they think it’s hard when something little happens to them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: You would not believe what I have been through if you saw it. Just little things you can't do, you give up. I was telling them, Dad and Mom, they did everything. Looking for things in the woods. Squirrels, rabbits, onion, and mushrooms. One time, my dad said, “There is a big black tree over there. Let’s go over there.” He took a piece of wood with a fork in it. It was long, so went in them old wagons that horses pulled. It was roads like that. We went on the side of the mountain where that tree was. It was blackjack. He was calling it a black tree. Way at the top was a mushroom this big [gesture] stuck on there. “I’m going to drop it. If it hits the ground and comes apart, try to catch it,” he said. He was sticking it, and it started to shake. It dropped. I was doing this [gesture] and it was hitting the branches. It came apart and I couldn’t catch it then. By doing that, they made it through long time ago. Nowadays, it’s easy how the children are growing up. It’s easy where they are. Where we grew up, it was hard.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: These children that are living now, they say McDonalds or Pizza Hut. Also, for instance, they won’t hardly eat beans or potatoes.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Really, the girl that’s ten years old never eats beans or bologna.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And those older grandkids of mine have never eaten fried potatoes. And the bread you make, they haven’t either. They won’t even try it. I will weeee... [gesture]. I will say to them, “Really?” We don’t like that they will say. Eat beans? No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I was growing up, “Eat what I put on the table,” I was told.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And that’s what we did, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you don’t like it, you are going to be starving, I was told. I was telling some of my grandkids, “Long time ago, we were just eating water gravy.” They were just laughing, “Gaw, really?” Yeah, they wouldn’t believe we ate like that growing up.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s still good, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ah, man.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: My grandmother would raise and can. What is the name, a mason jar, those. That’s what she would use and…

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did they plant lots of stuff?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They would preserve it, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They would dig a hole in the ground. They called it a gunny sack. That is what they would lay underneath. Then they would cover it back with dirt. I was telling my children. That boy, he doesn’t speak Cherokee. That boy I have, he is half white. He started school when he was three. He can understand Cherokee, but he can't speak it. I told him, “Let’s go build a fence.” When he was only about four, he could already understand what I was saying. He went and got a hammer and was waiting for me at the door. I remember a long time ago, we were at a ball game. They were called the Seventy-Sixers, Jack’s team.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was us, yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: That Linda Vann.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: And all of them and Littlejohn was also on that team.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, Mona.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, Linda and all them girls.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Boy, that Linda was fast.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, she was long-legged.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: She would go around quick. Yeah, I remember the one they called Baby Sis was one year behind in high school.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We still call her that Baby Sis. He talking about Marie.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They were the only good batters, I was telling them the first time we talked. I remember all of the past.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That what he is talking about. We were called the Seventy-Sixers when we first started.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They were really good, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We became good, but when we first started, they gave us a hard-luck trophy. Haaa, I said. Then we became pretty good. Those Greasy Indians, we wanted to defeat them all the time.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Who was the Ulisgvni sister that was on the other team? She was the catcher. She was Donald Adair’s sister.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, Louella.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: She was the catcher.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Squwolla, they called her.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: She was really good, and they were pitching fast.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were all really good ball players.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They would always be the best. Dave had a pretty good team, Dave Killer.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Senora was the coach. He was my uncle. Boy, I wanted to defeat him. I was the pitcher and sometimes they would call me to pitch. He would be getting on to me. I said, “Weee, I am never going to help you.” He would just be getting on to me.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: What about Virginia? Whose team was she on? I remember that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Her playing, too, didn’t she help us sometimes?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: That’s it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And Josephine.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Josephine and that other who is married to the preacher.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Betsy.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Sometimes they did help us.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Boy, they were fast. They would just go like this. [gesture]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We were running around.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They would be running over there, and the dust would be still right here. The boys had a team at Greasy. They were pretty good, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Charlie Shell was our coach for a little while.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was first, or maybe it was Jack first, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then it was Charlie, I think, as I remember.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: When I think that far back.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It’s great, ain’t it, to think about that?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I look there. I look towards the woods, but here I see it different.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Little Jack used to treat us real good. He was friendly.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: His wife would be standing nearby.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was friendly, too. Sometimes he would be drinking and be driving us around. He would be doing this, and we would be in the back. If you think about it sometimes now, it was dangerous for us.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: He didn’t have a daughter, did he?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They were all boys.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Five, wasn’t there? Five boys?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: There is just three alive now, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I think it was six.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Six. I guess it was little…

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Farris.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dexter.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah, and ah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Rex, David.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Frankie and the other one, Robbie.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Gaw, really, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: There was six of them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That Dexter Van, too?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I think so, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s a preacher. We are talking about his dad, Little Jack.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, well I’ll be.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was really friendly.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Him and Mom were good friends. If they said the Seventy-Sixers were going to play, we would go. My dad would have very little gas, but we would still go.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did you know that Rogers Maclemore, when we played, he always came over there? I was the pitcher. He would stand at the screen while I was pitching, and when we got done, he called me lefty. He would say, “Come here, lefty. We won some money.” He was betting on how many I was going to strike out. He would give me some and say, “Go buy something.” I thought it was pretty good when he would give me five dollars.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: It was a lot then.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then it was.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Five dollars was a lot of money.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When I would see him, I would think to myself, “We are going to win some money,” I would be thinking.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Nowadays do they still play?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don’t think so. I think that is a place where they eat.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They would schedule games there all the time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They really did.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: There was a team from Tahlequah that would enter called the Night Stalkers. In fastpitch, like Tubb Girdner and them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were good, too.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: And Dry Creek, they would have a good game with Dry Creek.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Them women were really good, too.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They were all kinfolks, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Them Bolins, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was really good back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was really good to think back.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They would cheer them. They would cheer the batters. You wouldn’t hear English. They would cheer them on in Cherokee, then. That Josephine’s dad, they called him Charlie Boy.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Hubert.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: He would be hollering, standing around, cheering them. He would be hollering loud, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: All in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Something.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That Betsy’s dad.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: If they made a mistake, he’d say, “You are doing it all wrong. Do it right!” He wasn’t leaving nothing out. He was cheering them on, and it was all in Cherokee. And the fans were cheering in Cherokee, and nowadays they will be hollering in English, ain’t it? When I was growing up, I was already past grade school, I was telling my children I was just around Cherokee speakers and was looking for Cherokee. But nowadays, no one will even speak Cherokee. They will say why? They don’t know how, nowadays.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now they will be full-blood Cherokee and say, “I don’t understand it.” Gah-lee, I think it’s embarrassing when they say that.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: What about what Gary Van said? One time, a long time ago, he was working at Tyson, and I was working there, and he talked to some Cherokee girls in Cherokee. “We don’t understand what you are saying. We don’t understand Cherokee,” they said, and Gary looked at them and said they are black as crows and don’t understand Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s what my grandma used to say. They are standing there like a crow and they still don’t understand Cherokee.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: That’s what Gary said. If I come where Gary is, we will talk all Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He works here.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: If I still see him standing somewhere, I think about what he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was probably flirting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I come from towards Kenwood, there were some at Wicklif school. It went to the eighth grade. They were really good in basketball. They spoke in all Cherokee, and when they went to a white school, they would be saying, “What are they saying?”

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: There at Kenwood where they feed the senior citizens, across from there used to be a ballfield. Is it still there?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they built a new building. It’s big, and they made a new ball field. They have it good now.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: So they built them a new place to feed them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know if you know Cody Hare. He used to live towards Kenwood a long time ago.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: And that preacher, too, the one that lives across the water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s, ah, Woodrow Ross you are thinking about.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: There, where the roof was, he said it was too flat. He was wanting it to be more like this [gestures]. I used to be a carpenter, and we went over there, about six of us, and there was water running right by his house. “Are there lots of crawdads in there?” I said. “Yeah, people look for them, and they catch all they want to.”, he said. Then one white guy, [in English] “You got lots of crawdads in this creek?”, he said [to Woodrow]. “Yeah, grasshoppers caught them all,” he told him. And that white guy, “Grasshoppers? You mean they eat crawdads, too?”, he said. He said that part in English. He looked at me and said, [in Cherokee] “There are people around here that are named Grasshopper, I am talking about them. He didn’t understand, that one up there,” he said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was just doing that to him, too, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I started laughing when he said that. I laughed hard, and that guy up there said, “That ain’t fair. I can’t understand what y’all are saying. I know youns talking about me," he said. If you are speaking Cherokee, some whites will really listen.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And some will get mad, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: “I know y’all are talking about me,” they will say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I worked at the clinic for several years. Where I’m from, there were two boys there. We were friends when they came. Boy, we would talk all in Cherokee. We would talk in the hall and laugh, and later I was called in the office. The boss kinda got mad. “I got lots of complaints,” he said. I said, “What about?” He said, “You guys talking in Cherokee and laughing. Them nurses think you guys are talking about them,” he said. I told him we got better things to talk about.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did they make y’all quit talking?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they tried, but we kept on talking. I told my friends they said I thought that was a place for us Cherokees.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Some won’t like it nowadays. That’s the way they are. If I talk to somebody right here, and if there are whites there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do they get upset?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They will be looking toward you and doing this. [Facial expression]

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They will make fun of you.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Those whites, they will try to say the same thing, and laugh. That’s when I know they are making fun of us, when they say that when we Cherokee speakers are gone, you are not going to hear anyone speak Cherokee anymore. I tell them children, and even now if it was my Cherokee friends’ kids, I tell them what I have seen. And you won’t see what I have seen a long time ago. Y’all are missing a lot of things, I was telling them. We were poor growing up, but it was also good back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes I think of how poor we grew up back then. For instance, when we went to town, we didn’t lock the doors.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: No, it was the same with us.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And also there was a bucket hanging on the porch. When they were thirsty, they would get a drink. And there was unity back then. Now it don’t hardly exist. Unity, they call it.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: How water comes to the house now, it wasn’t like that. It was about the year ‘71 or ‘72 when they put water in. That’s when they built the house for my mom and dad, those first Indian homes. It was just made of wood. Dad milled and built four corners: living room, kitchen, and we had our beds here. We didn’t have lights then either. Back then, it was around ‘71, someone came and said, “Cherokee Nation are building houses. Sign here and I will fill it out.” They knew Mom didn’t understand. “Just put your name or put an x there, and I will be the witness,” he said. And they put an x and he witnessed it. “I am going to take this paper to Cherokee Nation. I’m not saying when they are going to start.” Within three months, they came and measured where they were going to build. In about two weeks, they brought things like a bulldozer, and they built it for them. And then we seen lights.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You know, it was good that those people came all the way out there, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I don’t remember where he came from, but he was a Cherokee Nation worker who came there. It might’ve been from the school ‘cause a bus would go by from Rocky Mountain. Probably one of them said something.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s right, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: “They need a new house,” they said. There were nine of us at the time.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Someone that works here was telling me yesterday, they said they have been waiting fourteen years for them to build a house, and now they said OK. Gaw!!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When me and my wife first got married, we signed up to get a house built, but the head person was really against us. I don’t know why, he kinda acted like a white man, because his wife was white. Then we said, “Let’s go to FHA.” So we went there. It wasn’t two weeks before they said, “Y’all go look for a house.” And we found one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Where y’all live now?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We started paying it and we paid it off a long time ago. We got help from the whites. Sometimes there were some that would go against you, and some you said would help you quickly.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Them old ones a long time ago, they helped each other. They would cut wood all day, and the next week they would do the same thing. They helped each other, those elders that lived then. And nowadays, they will say, “He’s on his own.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don’t know if you have also seen, for instance, when someone passed away, they would have a wake service at their house.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: All night.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: People would be sitting there all night. They would be singing and talking about what they did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And the men would have a fire built outside, drinking coffee and talking all night.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They don’t do that now, do they?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They will just go for a little while, and they won’t keep the body at their house, just at the funeral home. They will just view them for a little while.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, maybe for an hour or two they will view him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was telling the children, “When I die, I don’t want anyone viewing me,” I was telling them. I said, “Keep it closed.” They were looking at me. I said, “No, I’m saying what’s right. I don’t want someone looking at me and saying oowee,” I was telling them.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Those kids would say, “I want to go somewhere. I am lonesome.” They have lots of things to play with, and when we were growing up, we would use wood or a rock to play with and pretend it was a car. We would be pushing around a rock.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time we talked to a certain person here, and I asked, “What did you have to play with when you were growing up?” He said, “Not much of anything. All we had was some shoes. We dragged around those they call loafers. We pretended they were convertibles.” There were shoes like that back then. I guess there still is.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And those bicycles. They made basketball rims from them, they said, the tires.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: It would be hanging there bent, when we started. That’s the way we had it, and it was easy for it to bend.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Y’all were probably dunking it.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Just by using that, we got pretty good at school. We would make shots from far away. It was easy for us with the rim on there good. Them whites didn’t hardly know how to play, but Cherokees were pretty good because of growing up like that. My dad would take the tires off himself, when he had a flat. There would be wires sticking out of his tires. It was just ten or fifteen dollars for a tire back then, but that was hard to find. If someone took their tires off, they would ask Mom and Dad if they wanted them, and he would take them. They used to put tubes in them back then. And the tires he took, we thought it was great. We would be playing with them, pretending they were cars. We would roll them around in the woods. We played with things like that growing up, but nowadays, I’m amazed they have all that stuff they bought from Walmart, and they will say, “I am lonesome, let’s go somewhere.” They just want to go riding around, I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And also, children will really cry for something, and when you give it to them, they will play with it for a little while, and then it will be scattered everywhere.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’ll say. They will have things scattered.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you were talking about tires, we used to push those around. We would put dirt in them. When we pushed them, dust would be flying around.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: When you said dust would be flying around, I remembered my grandma had two horses that pulled a plow. She had a boy named Snow. He was my uncle. He got sick. That’s what he was using to plow. He couldn’t do anything anymore, and he gave one to my dad. I don’t know if you remember him. He was about four years old, and his name was John Ketcher. He said, “That’s going to be my horse. You can’t ride. It’s just going to pull.” “I’m going to break it,” my dad said. “He’s going to ride around.” “I already broke it,” he said. I was standing right there. He just made a rope, and as soon as he laid it on there, that horse kicked. That ash they took from the wood stove setting outside, he landed in there. That ash flew up. That ash flew up. I remembered that when you said dust.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was acting good.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: We laughed, Beverly was there, too. She was laughing. We were looking at each other. He got mad. “Y’all stop laughing at me! The same thing is going to happen to y’all. I’m going to put y’all on this horse!” We got quiet.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Beverly is the only girl, ain’t it? Or is there another?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Peggy is the other, and oldest name is Wanda. She was fifty-two when she died. Diabetes killed her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, I remember her.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Her son was laying down with covers on, and when Wanda walked by, she tripped and broke her hip. They fixed it here in Tahlequah, and when she went to rehab, they would lay her down and take her shoe off. And this, too. At rehab, they said they would loosen it up. She was scraping it on the carpet, and she got a...

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: A sore.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: She got a sore. Then they took all the meat off. The bones were like balls, marbles. They bandaged it. They didn’t know yet if it was going to heal. I thought nothing would happen. The bone was showing ‘cause she showed it to me. It was turning black, and they cut it off here. It was still black all the way up to her knee, and up to here [gesture]. They said, “That’s as far as we can go.” She was like it was burnt. She was barely hanging in there. Then they sent her to Tulsa. “We can’t do anything. All we can do is give her painkillers,” they said. But she said... they told us this Wanda could speak English. The doctor put us in a room and told us what it was doing, and he said, “She wants to go home because she knows she is going to die. She wants to spend the night at her house before she goes.” “It’s OK, I will take her home now," my mom said. Mom said it in Cherokee and when he heard it, he got up and said, “I will take her now. We are going to make arrangements for what they call hospice. They will take care of her all night and all day. I don’t really know how long she is going to live. It might be a day or it might be three days,” he said. But when they brought her back, the people that were going to take care of her were already there. She would just sleep. They would just rub something sweet on her to check her sugar.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was low, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: But they said her heart rate was starting to get slower. They were always checking it. And lots of her friends would visit. Hospice brought a bed into the living room. She was laying there. She would have her eyes closed. When they would do it, she would open them and close them. That was all she would do, and her friends, those Pettits, they would sing Cherokee. They were friends, like Bob Pettit and them, they can sing good Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: All those boys, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: She used to schedule them for somebody’s birthday when Mom and Dad were still alive. She already had a new house, built back in eighty-two, I think it was. That’s where they would schedule them, Bob and singers from Bell. There would be lots of people there singing. She would serve them a huge dinner. Nowadays, they don’t do that. All that I don’t see anymore, things that they used to do, and my youngest daughter, I told her, “When I pass away...” And those who are the same age are the last of us Cherokee speakers. They are teaching them. I didn’t know if it’s going to happen, but us fluent speakers, as soon as we pass on, it’s going to be gone. The youngest daughter has been around Wanda the most while she was growing up, while I was working.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was watching her. They really done her wrong. They should have been watching how they were doing her foot.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Yeah, when they were doing that she was scraping it. There was kinda like water coming out of it. Then she remembered. She said, “When I was going to the doctor, they would lay me down and do my feet like this, and that’s when it started, where the carpet was laying”. But after that, when they started cutting on her, she didn’t last long. One time I called her, but she had just gone in. I called her room number in Tulsa. I said, “What did the doctors find?” They said “I would not get better. They talked about how I could pass on. They said there is nothing they can do. ‘But you still have a small chance,’ “they told her.” I told Mom, and she said “oo wee Let’s go there”. And we went there and stayed about three days. We couldn’t hardly sleep, so we came home. I took time off. I used a leave so when we got back, I called her the next day. The phone was ringing but she wasn’t answering. “Something might have happened. Call her back,” Mom told me. So I called her back. Then the doctor was in the room. “Hello, I’m looking for Wanda Ketcher, my sister,” I told him. He said, “She is not able to talk, she is in the cycle now.” Then we charged over there. By then, she didn’t know anything. And like I said a while ago how the doctor told us what she wanted, that’s what happened, and she spent the night. It was around six or six thirty when I went to give Mom’s dogs water and food, and Mom looked out and said, “She’s finished. She is gone.” I walked over there, and those that were watching her already had her covered up. They said, “We are just waiting on the hearse.” While they were waiting that long, they were singing in Cherokee, and when they came to get her, there were cars lined up to the funeral home. And at the funeral home, they were all around. They said, “We are going to have to fix her.” When they put them in the cooler, they said, they have to do that so she don’t go bad. This is just her shell. She is already gone. So then everyone left. The other one I was talking about, John, diabetes killed him, too. The same thing happened to him. He got his little toe cut off. He was told to go on dialysis. When he got back, really... Wanda used to go. I seen something happen when Wanda was going, because I would take her. He said John really did drive. He would take her over there and go get her, and seeing that he didn’t want to go to dialysis, he didn’t tell nobody he wasn’t going. The doctors were looking for him. We had to watch him good when he got his little toe cut off. That is where gangrene starts. He said it was already too late. It was about six days before they found him with an old lady that was in our kinfolk’s house. He was already asleep hard. They couldn’t wake him up. He passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was that coma, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: But he chose that himself. Mom was still alive when he passed away. Me and Mom were sitting there. He said, “I’m not going through what Wanda went through. How they drew blood from her, they are not going to do that to me.” That day, he passed. He chose what happened to him. He didn’t want to be given different blood. They change it, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They say some pass away while they are doing that to them. How long do they go in there when they do that to them?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: For Wanda it was a little over... it’s different, two or three hours she would go in there. Boy, you could smell that blood where they were. Sometimes, John would go in where they had lots of beds. I looked in there once or twice. They had beds and they had them hooked up. It would smell like blood where they were, so when John saw all that, he didn’t want to do that. “I can’t go through that,” he told Mom. He got in his car quietly, and he left. That was the last time we seen him. When we seen him again, I guess you could say he was already dead. When the ambulance took him to Stilwell, they sent him to Tulsa and Tulsa said we can’t do anything, his brain is already dead.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was like that for too long, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah. I had a younger brother. They started hooking him up to that. One time... I used to stop at Mom’s. I would stop there. They lived together, and also my brother that I’m talking about. He was rolling around on the floor. He was uncomfortable that they were taking blood from him. He was saying, “I wish someone would shoot me.” I said, “Why? Let’s keep praying.” We would pray and then I would go to work. Then, one time, ‘cause he had to go three times to Miami, then they would draw blood from him to clean it. Then I think we had to go there on a Saturday. He went in for a little while, and he came back. Before, he used to go in there for three hours. He was coming back - his name was Ogan in Cherokee. Everybody called him Ogan, even the whites as well. They would say, “Hi, Ogan.” I said, “What is it, Ogan?” He got back in [the car?]. “They said I didn’t have to go through dialysis,” he said. He never had to go to dialysis again.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It was getting better.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, but after about four years, he became ill. Then he passed. He lived for that long. I was amazed by it. I said, “What did the doctors say?” The head doctor came from Tulsa and checked him, and he said, “Andrew, you don’t have to be on dialysis. Go on home.” He had a good life for that long. This talk we are having, you said a while ago how Cherokee is fading away. The intention is not for it to fade away. Those that are going to this school might learn something from your conversation. They are trying to save the Cherokee language so that it doesn’t run out. But also, they are going to have to battle. Some are really… the Cherokee that the children are speaking here sounds a little different, and how we speak it has low and high sounds, but this is just straight. And also, we use our hands when we talk about something, and we kinda make facial expressions. If it’s important or funny, the learners are just straight.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: When we speak Cherokee, when we use our hands, what we are talking about is what we are seeing. That’s what a store owner asked me one time. Do you remember Claude Eubanks? He said, “Larry, lots of people come in,” he asked me in English, “lots people come in here. You are the only one that I noticed you use your hands when you talk.” Yeah even when I speak in English, I can see it. That’s why I use my hands. That’s how the elders are. That’s what the elders used. That’s where I learned it. I told him, “What we see when we speak, we can see what we are talking about.” “Yeah, that’s what I didn’t understand,” he told me. And those others would have their hands in their pockets, talking same as you said the students who talk straight. That’s it. If they can see what they are talking about, they will start using Cherokee.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And if something is funny, we see it even funnier. Like you said, if someone falls down, we will just start laughing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We will start laughing at them.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They will say to you, “What if that was you?”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: “You fell down,” we would be saying.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: “Are you hurting, I am hurting.” Like you said, we use the sound when we speak.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Mom and Dad would say something to the oldest one named Jimmy Ray. He’s still alive. He is about seventy-two or three years old. He speaks fluent, too. We all are fluent. It was Beverly that used to act like she was white. She can speak though.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Has she not been here?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She should come, or they all should come.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I don’t think any of them have been here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You might tell them.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: They can all speak Cherokee. They would tell about all the things I have done.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Are you afraid to tell them?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: “Don’t tell about me,” I will tell them. The one that’s born behind me, his name is Charles, and behind him is Quinton. His name is Dvdovni and Charles, his Cherokee name in English is Skunk. They called him that growing up, those whites. He is about sixty years, and when they see him they will say, “What you been doing, Skunk?” Really, as we were going to school, everyone called him that. Dad named him. Our bathroom wasn’t inside the building. It was way over there. He used to be afraid to go outside by himself, and he would go in his pants, and in the mornings, that’s when Dad named him Dili - Skunk.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, my brother’s name was Ogan. Even in English, they called him Ogan and in Cherokee it was Ogan. The reason they named him Ogan, it was Groundhog Day when he was born.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: What about Bigfoot? Do y’all believe that?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: South from where I'm from, where they call it Cloud, they were looking for it. Even someone from the TV station was parked there, looking for him. I had to go preach there at New Clouds. They were there looking for him, and when we were coming back, I was wondering why the cars were parked there. They were parked on the side of the road in the dark. They said, “They are looking for Bigfoot.” But I don’t know, I don’t really know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What do you think?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What do you think about that?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: One time, me and Dili – Skunk – were hunting. We were about twelve. My dad had some coon dogs. We went a long ways up a mountain, where we were heading below and we had already gone a long way and you know how it turns foggy? That’s what it was doing. We were walking and we couldn’t hardly see anything. We were on a road where a car had been. We had about six dogs. They got in a fight with something, and the dogs got whipped. Where we were standing, them dogs came running into us. One almost knocked me down. We had a twenty-two [rifle]. I was carrying it. Something was coming and those dogs were scared. Some took off running but one stayed. Something was coming towards us, but we couldn’t see anything. Just right there where the door is, that was where the fog was, that low. It was coming. I thought “If I stop right here, they can’t see me.” So I stopped. Dili was saying “What! What!” He was standing right there. I had that gun like this [gesture]. I turned back. “What! What!” “I don’t know, I don’t know what it is,” I told him. It just went around us. It was walking on two feet from the sound. He was saying, “Shoot it! Shoot it! Shoot it!” he was telling me. It went around, and when it got where it started, it walked away. We never did see what it was. If it was a bear, it would’ve been on all fours, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It would have made a sound if it was a bear, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: I don’t know if someone was just trying to scare us, that’s why I didn’t shoot. He was saying, “Shoot it! Shoot it!” He was hollering and scared. He was grabbing me here [gesture]. That’s all I remember that happened. I think about that when they talk about Bigfoot nowadays. When they see it. But I didn’t see what it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me, a long time ago, when I was a little boy, like you said, my grandmother she had a strawberry patch. We went to Anderson and, like you said, I can’t remember how much they were paying us a day. They just had a small patch. We were fixing it. There was a house there. They let us stay in it. There was a hollow close by, and the old lady heard something. And the dogs started barking. There were two dogs staying there at the time. They were barking, and she said, “I wonder what it is?” So I went that way. What did she call it in Cherokee? What did she call him? Yauwe, or something, she called it, and it was dragging something. He was using something made of wood to drag. “He was dragging that in the hollow,” she said. And then at night, when we went to sleep, she would put food on the eating table. She would say, “It won’t hardly bother you.” When she did put something up there, in the morning someone would have eaten it. I would wake up late in the night and hear plates and forks. Like you said, I didn’t know what it was. And then one time, we went to town. There was an old man working there. He had horses, and that old man remembered me, and he thought, “I am going to go get that boy and go horseback riding,” he said. I was going there, and rocks were landing close by. He kept going, and still more rocks were landing close by. He said it scared him, so he turned around. I asked my grandmother, and she said, “Something is watching out here,” she said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: People really do talk about seeing Bigfoot. I have never seen him. I don’t think I want to see him.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: Do you know Lee Sevenstar?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: He believes it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: He said he has seen him. And Bob Pettit’s younger brother, Watie is his name, and Bob said Watie seen it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, they talk about seeing it.

segments.speaker: larry-don-ketcher
segments.translation: One time, he was working right there, Lee Sevenstar, at the housing authority. Until he retired, he was working there. And there was a white man there. He found out Lee believed in that. And you know where they are making a new road up that hill on the other side towards Jay? That white man was out that way, and he came back in the evening, almost quitting time. He came back and said, “Lee, this old woman ran over Bigfoot this morning past Euchie Lake. Right when you cross Euchie Lake going up that hill, it jumped in front of her and bent one side of her car,” he told him. And Lee said, “Did they kill it?” He said, “No, it was dragging its feet, and it went across the hollow. That steep place on this side, he went off in there,” he told him. The next day, Lee was waiting for him to get there. He said, “Did they ever find that Bigfoot?” he asked that white man. Lee can speak good English. He said, “No, but they seen it again, they said, this morning.” He said they did. Yeah, it went back across. “This time, it was in a wheelchair,” he told him. Lee got mad! ‘Cause he believed it. He was joking with him. Boy, Lee got mad about it. “Yeah, they seen it again this morning before work. I stopped at that Kansas store and they were talking about it,” he said. There is a store in Little Kansas. “They were talking about it. They seen it again this morning, they said. When it went across, it was in a wheelchair.” Boy, Lee got mad at him for good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, I appreciate it.
